question.:question/problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+6y=3{e}^{5x}.
$$

Select the correct options below.$\,$ An integrating factor for this equation is $I(x)=$ {{field-1}}.

$\,$ The general solution is given by $y(x)=$ {{field-2}}.
question.:question/worked-solution:
This equation is already in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x)
$$

with $P(x)=6$ and $Q(x)=3{e}^{5x}.$ We proceed to find an integrating factor $I(x)$ using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int 6\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{6x}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we multiply our differential equation through by $I(x)={e}^{6x}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{6x}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+6y) & ={e}^{6x}\cdot 3{e}^{5x} \\ {e}^{6x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+6{e}^{6x}\cdot y & =3{e}^{11x}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we rewrite the left hand side as $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y\cdot I(x))$ and carry out the integration:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{e}^{6x}) & =3{e}^{11x} \\ \int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{e}^{6x})\text{d}x & =\int 3{e}^{11x}\,\text{d}x \\ y{e}^{6x} & =\frac{3{e}^{11x}}{11}+C \\ y & =\frac{3{e}^{5x}}{11}+C{e}^{-6x}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{6x}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+6y) & ={e}^{6x}\cdot x{e}^{-6x} \\ {e}^{6x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+6{e}^{6x}\cdot y & =x\end{aligned}

question.:question/problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{6}{x}y=3,\,x>0.
$$

Select the correct options below:

$\,$ An integrating factor for this equation is $I(x)=$ {{field-1}}.

$\,$ The general solution is given by $y(x)=$ {{field-2}}.
question.:question/worked-solution:
This equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x)
$$

with $P(x)=\frac{6}{x}$ and $Q(x)=3.$ We proceed to find an integrating factor $I(x)$ using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,dx} \\  & ={e}^{\int (6/x)\,dx} \\  & ={e}^{6\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{6})} \\  & ={x}^{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we multiply our differential equation through by $I(x)={x}^{6}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{6}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{6}{x}y) & ={x}^{6}\cdot 3 \\ {x}^{6}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+6{x}^{5}y & =3{x}^{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we rewrite the left hand side as $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y\cdot I(x))$ and carry out the integration:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{d}{dx}(y{x}^{6})\,dx & =\int 3{x}^{6}\,\text{d}x \\ y{x}^{6} & =\frac{3{x}^{7}}{7}+C \\ y & =\frac{3x}{7}+\frac{C}{{x}^{6}}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{6}{x}y=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{{x}^{5}},\,x>0.
$$

Select the correct options below.$\,$ An integrating factor for this equation is $I(x)=$ {{field-1}}.

$\,$ The general solution is given by $y(x)=$ {{field-2}}.
question.:question/worked-solution:
This equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x)
$$

with $P(x)=\frac{6}{x}$ and $Q(x)=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{{x}^{5}}.$ We proceed to find an integrating factor $I(x)$ using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (6/x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{6\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & ={x}^{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we multiply our differential equation through by $I(x)={x}^{6}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{6}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{6}{x}y) & ={x}^{6}\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{{x}^{5}} \\ {x}^{6}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+6{x}^{5}y & =x\operatorname{sin}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we rewrite the left hand side as $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y\cdot I(x))$ and carry out the integration:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{x}^{6}) & =x\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ \int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{x}^{6})\text{d}x & =\int x\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

To solve this integral, we integrate by parts. 

$$
\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x=uv-\int {u}^{′}v\,\text{d}x
$$

Let $u=x,{u}^{′}=1,{v}^{′}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x,$ and $v=-\operatorname{cos}⁡x.$ Then, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y{x}^{6} & =\int x\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\ y{x}^{6} & =x(-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-\int (-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\cdot 1\,\text{d}x \\ y{x}^{6} & =-x\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\ y{x}^{6} & =-x\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,+C \\ y & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{{x}^{6}}-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{{x}^{5}}+\frac{C}{{x}^{6}}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the differential equation
$6\frac{dy}{dx} + y = 2x$.
Select the correct options below.
An integrating factor for this equation is $I(x) =$ {{field-1}}.

The general solution is given by $y(x) =$ {{field-2}}.
question.:question/worked-solution:
First divide the equation by $6$ to write it in standard form.

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{6}y=\frac{x}{3}
$$

This equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x)
$$

with $P(x)=\frac{1}{6}$ and $Q(x)=\frac{x}{3}.$ We proceed to find an integrating factor $I(x)$ using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int 1/6\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{x/6}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we multiply our differential equation through by $I(x)={e}^{x/6}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{x/6}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{6}y) & ={e}^{x/6}\cdot \frac{x}{3} \\ {e}^{x/6}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{6}{e}^{x/6}\cdot y & =\frac{x}{3}{e}^{x/6}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we rewrite the left hand side as $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y\cdot I(x))$ and carry out the integration:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{e}^{x/6}) & =\frac{x}{3}{e}^{x/6} \\ \int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{e}^{x/6})\text{d}x & =\int \frac{x}{3}{e}^{x/6}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

To solve this integral, we integrate by parts.

$$
\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x=uv-\int {u}^{′}v\,\text{d}x
$$

Let $u=x,{u}^{′}=1,{v}^{′}={e}^{x/6},$ and $v=6{e}^{x/6}.$ Then, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y{e}^{x/6} & =\int \frac{x}{3}{e}^{x/6}\,\text{d}x \\ y{e}^{x/6} & =\frac{2}{6}\left(x(6{e}^{x/6})-\int 6{e}^{x/6}\,\text{d}x\right) \\ y{e}^{x/6} & =2x{e}^{x/6}-2\int {e}^{x/6}\,\text{d}x \\ y{e}^{x/6} & =2x{e}^{x/6}-12{e}^{x/6}+C \\ y{e}^{x/6} & =2(x-6){e}^{x/6}+C \\ y & =2(x - 6) + Ce^{-x/6}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-3y=6{e}^{2x}.
$$

Select the correct options below.$\,$ An integrating factor for this equation is $I(x)=$ {{field-1}}.

$\,$ The general solution is given by $y(x)=$ {{field-2}}.
question.:question/worked-solution:
This equation is already in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x)
$$

with $P(x)=-3$ and $Q(x)=6{e}^{2x}.$ We proceed to find an integrating factor $I(x)$ using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int -3\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{-3x}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we multiply our differential equation through by $I(x)={e}^{-3x}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{-3x}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-3y) & ={e}^{-3x}\cdot 6{e}^{2x} \\ {e}^{-3x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-3{e}^{-3x}\cdot y & =6{e}^{-x}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we rewrite the left hand side as $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y\cdot I(x))$ and carry out the integration:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{e}^{-3x}) & =6{e}^{-x} \\ \int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{e}^{-3x})\text{d}x & =\int 6{e}^{-x}\,\text{d}x \\ y{e}^{-3x} & =-6{e}^{-x}+C \\ y & =-6{e}^{2x}+C{e}^{3x}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-4y=5{e}^{x}.
$$

Select the correct options below.$\,$ An integrating factor for this equation is $I(x)=$ {{field-1}}.

$\,$ The general solution is given by $y(x)=$ {{field-2}}.
question.:question/worked-solution:
This equation is already in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x)
$$

with $P(x)=-4$ and $Q(x)=5{e}^{x}.$ We proceed to find an integrating factor $I(x)$ using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int -4\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{-4x}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we multiply our differential equation through by $I(x)={e}^{-4x}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{-4x}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-4y) & ={e}^{-4x}\cdot 5{e}^{x} \\ {e}^{-4x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-4{e}^{-4x}\cdot y & =5{e}^{-3x}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we rewrite the left hand side as $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y\cdot I(x))$ and carry out the integration:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{e}^{-4x}) & =5{e}^{-3x} \\ \int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{e}^{-4x})\text{d}x & =\int 5{e}^{-3x}\,\text{d}x \\ y{e}^{-4x} & =-\frac{5{e}^{-3x}}{3}+C \\ y & =-\frac{5{e}^{x}}{3}+C{e}^{4x}\end{aligned}
$$
